newsitem.title: GABON: Zaire's Mobutu delays return home for Mbeki talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu delays return home for Mbeki talks.

text.p: South Africa's Vice-President Thabo Mbeki headed for Gabon on Friday and talks with Zaire's embattled president Mobutu Sese Seko, after winning a pledge from rebel leader Laurent Kabila to give diplomacy a chance.

Mobutu, who is battling cancer and Kabila's rebels, delayed his return to Kinshasa for the talks with Mbeki, which will lay the groundwork for another face-to-face meeting between the civil war rivals on a South African ship on Wednesday.
"Mr Kabila says he is committed to the peaceful resolution of the Zaire conflict," Mbeki told reporters in Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi after talks with the rebel leader.
"He is willing to give diplomacy a chance and our understanding is he will not proceed with the military campaign until after next week's meeting," he added.
Earlier, as two more international airlines cancelled flights to Kinshasa, the rebels restated their demand that Mobutu stand down and hand power to Kabila.
"We insist as we have always insisted that Mr Mobutu must resign and hand over power directly to 'President' Kabila," rebel "foreign minister" Bizima Karaha said in Lubumbashi.
There was little fresh news from the war front. Last reports of the rebel advance spoke of a bloody battle at the start of the week at Kenge, around 250 km (155 miles) from Kinshasa.

Mbeki is shuttling round Africa as part of efforts to head off a bloody battle for Zaire's capital. He is trying to build on talks between Mobutu and Kabila hosted by Nelson Mandela on a South African ship on Sunday.
He said Kabila had agreed to meet Mobutu on a South African navy ship again on Wednesday and he assumed Mobutu would attend.
Karaha accused French-speaking Central African presidents who held a mini-summit in Libreville with Mobutu on Thursday of "playing games and trying to protect Mobutu".
The summit foresaw a key role for Zaire's parliament and urged early replacement of its speaker -- the constitutional successor in the event of Mobutu's death or incapacity.
"We cannot be fooled," Karaha said. "The proposal is absolute nonsense to us."

The U.S. television network CNN reported from Kinshasa that Mbeki was carrying a new peace plan that envisaged parliament electing a speaker to whom Mobutu could hand power and who in return could hand over to another leader.

Officials in Kinshasa had said that Mobutu would return home on Friday. Mobutu's spokesman in Gabon expected Friday's talks with Mbeki to last around 40 minutes. Officials expected Mobutu to return to Kinshasa on Saturday.
Mobutu's fellow French-speaking Central African presidents welcomed his decision not to seek re-election, saying it opened a way for a peaceful end to the war.

France, a longtime Mobutu ally, expressed similar hopes. Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said in Paris the mini-summit "opened new prospects for an orderly and peaceful transition, based on the regular functioning of institutions".

The United Nations accused the rebels on Friday of blocking an investigation into alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire by denying U.N. investigators and forensic experts access to rebel-controlled areas to dig up mass graves.

Belgian airline Sabena has cancelled all stops at Kinshasa and is diverting its flights to Congo's capital Brazzaville. Ethiopian Airlines also cancelled its flights and diverted them to Togo's capital Lome. Swissair has switched to Brazzaville.
